learn.title: Planetary Physics Lab — What if…?
learn.subtitle: Local SI-unit simulators connected to your selected body and site. Compare Earth, Mars, and the Moon with explicit equations and limits.
learn.noComparisonHint: Select an Earth H3 cell in Compare to link real terrestrial slope measurements to these challenges.

weight.question: Does your mass change if you travel to Mars or the Moon?
weight.intro: Mass (kg) is invariant; what changes is gravitational force or weight (N).
weight.limits: Assumptions: standard mean surface gravity (Earth 9.80665; Mars 3.71; Moon 1.62 m/s²). A spring scale calibrated on Earth would read lower kgf, not lower mass.

jump.question: How high would you jump with the same takeoff speed?
jump.intro: At equal takeoff velocity, peak height scales inversely with g.
jump.limits: Ideal vertical model without air drag or pressurized spacesuit load. On Mars (~2.64×) and the Moon (~6.05×), suit mass and biomechanics limit real impulse.

projectile.question: How does a projectile parabola change across worlds?
projectile.intro: Ideal ballistic trajectory without aerodynamic drag from the same launch height.
projectile.svgLabel: Comparison of parabolic trajectories on Earth, Mars, and Moon
projectile.limits: No atmospheric drag; ideal max range occurs at 45° and does not depend on mass in this model. On Earth, air slows light projectiles.

waves.question: What happens to waves in a pool inside a pressurized habitat?
waves.intro: Simulated inside a pressurized, thermally controlled habitat (not outdoors on Mars).
waves.limits: Valid only in the shallow-water regime (depth d ≪ wavelength λ): on Mars wave speed is ~0.615× (~38.5% slower). Deep-water waves depend on λ.

rocks.question: Is it equally easy to accelerate a rock even if it weighs less?
rocks.intro: Lifting against gravity takes less force, but horizontal acceleration requires the exact same net force F = m·a.
rocks.limits: Inertia (mass) does not decrease on Mars or the Moon. Lower weight also reduces maximum static friction with the ground.

rover.question: How does gravity affect a rover climbing a slope?
rover.intro: Inclined-plane force decomposition linked to the slopes of the active site and Earth analog.
rover.limits: Ideal rigid model (tan θ ≤ μ). In real Martian/lunar regolith or loose Atacama sand, wheel sinkage and soil cohesion reduce traction before the ideal limit.
rover.diagramLabel: Interactive free-body force diagram for rover on a {{slope}}-degree slope

wind.question: Does a 100 km/h wind on Mars push as hard as on Earth?
wind.intro: Dynamic pressure scales with air density ρ: Mars atmosphere is ~60× less dense than Earth.
wind.limits: Illustrative mean surface densities (Earth ~1.225 kg/m³; Mars ~0.020 kg/m³). Real density varies with elevation, temperature, and season.

water.question: What happens to open-air liquid water in Antofagasta vs Mars?
water.intro: Liquid water stability depends on both pressure and temperature; Martian pressure (~0.61 kPa) sits right near the triple point.
water.limits: Educational approximation using water triple point (0.611657 kPa; 0.01 °C) and Clausius-Clapeyron relation. Brines (Atacama salts or Martian perchlorates) shift freezing points.

curiosities.pressureTitle: Liquid water outdoors on Mars (~0.6 kPa)
curiosities.pressureDesc: Unlike Antofagasta (~101 kPa at sea level), Martian surface pressure is ~0.6 kPa: exposed liquid water boils, freezes, or sublimates depending on temperature.
curiosities.dustDesc: Even with fast winds, Mars thin atmosphere (~1% of Earth density) produces lower dynamic pressure q = 0.5·ρ·v² at the same wind speed.
curiosities.atacamaTitle: Why is Atacama / Yungay a key analog?
curiosities.atacamaDesc: Extreme hyperaridity, UV flux, and saline soils allow studying Mars-analog processes, while gravity (1 g), pressure, and cosmic radiation remain irreproducible.
curiosities.soundTitle: Sound on Mars (~240 m/s and attenuated)
curiosities.soundDesc: In Mars thin CO₂ atmosphere (~0.6 kPa), sound travels around 240 m/s (vs ~343 m/s on Earth) and high frequencies attenuate rapidly. Speaking outdoors without a suit is unsafe.
curiosities.solTitle: A Martian sol lasts 24 h 39 min (vs 29.5 days on the Moon)
curiosities.solDesc: A Martian sol is just 39 minutes longer than an Earth day, whereas the lunar day/night cycle lasts ~29.5 Earth days, challenging solar power storage.
curiosities.commsTitle: Earth–Mars signal delay (3 to 22 min one-way)
curiosities.commsDesc: Depending on orbital distance (55 to 401 million km), radio signals take ~3 to ~22 minutes each way—requiring local autonomous rover navigation.

mass.question: 1. If a 70 kg student travels to Jezero Crater, what happens to their mass and weight?
mass.optA: Mass drops to ~26 kg and weight stays 686 N
mass.optB: Mass stays 70 kg and weight drops to ~260 N
mass.optC: Both mass and weight drop to one-third
mass.explanation: Mass is intrinsic (70 kg). Weight is gravitational force P = m·g ≈ 70 × 3.71 ≈ 259.7 N.

roverDynamic.question: 2. At the active slope ({{slope}}°) near {{site}}, what happens to a 100 kg rover compared to Earth?
roverDynamic.optA: It climbs with higher traction because it weighs less
roverDynamic.optB: Parallel force drops (from {{earthN}} N to {{marsN}} N), but normal force also drops (to {{marsNormalN}} N on Mars)
roverDynamic.optC: A 15° slope is universally safe on any terrain
roverDynamic.explanation: Lower gravity reduces parallel force ({{earthN}} N → {{marsN}} N), but also lowers normal force ({{marsNormalN}} N) and max friction μ·N.

nonReplicable.question: 3. Which Mars variable CANNOT be replicated in open-air field trials in Antofagasta?
nonReplicable.optB: Surface UV irradiance and low relative humidity
nonReplicable.optC: Gravity (0.38 g), ~0.6 kPa CO₂ atmosphere, and ionizing GCR radiation
nonReplicable.explanation: Irreproducible breakage boundaries B (gravity, atmospheric pressure, cosmic radiation) cannot be replicated in open Earth field trials.

distributions.question: 4. What does it mean when two slope distributions are similar between Jezero and Atacama?
distributions.optA: Both sites are identical for landing without further tests
distributions.optB: Partial morphological similarity in an independent variable X, not full physical equivalence
distributions.explanation: Ckepi decouples X, Y, and B: geometric slope similarity never implies complete environmental or mechanical equivalence.

sound.q: Why would your voice sound different and much quieter on Mars?
sound.a: In Mars thin CO₂ atmosphere (~0.6 kPa), sound travels at ~240 m/s (vs ~343 m/s on Earth) and high frequencies attenuate quickly.

sol.q: How long is a day on Mars?
sol.a: One Martian sol lasts 24 h 39 min 35 s—almost identical to an Earth day, which helps teams schedule rover operations.

comms.q: Can you drive a Mars rover with a live joystick from Earth?
comms.a: No: depending on orbital distance, radio signals take ~3 to ~22 minutes one-way, so rovers rely on onboard autonomous navigation.

radiation.q: How much radiation does an astronaut face on Mars?
radiation.a: Without a global magnetic field or thick atmosphere, surface radiation far exceeds Earths ~2.4 mSv/yr average.

olympus.q: How tall is Olympus Mons compared to Atacama volcanoes?
olympus.a: It rises ~21.9 km high (~3× Everest) and spans ~600 km wide, yet its average slope is surprisingly gentle (~5°).

temperature.q: How much can temperature swing in a single Martian day?
temperature.a: In craters like Jezero or Gale, diurnal temperature swings exceed 60–80 K due to low thermal inertia and thin air.

blueSunset.q: What color are sunsets on Mars?
blueSunset.a: Bluish near the Sun: fine Martian dust scatters red light at wide angles while letting blue light pass forward.

phobos.q: Which way does Phobos rise and set in the Martian sky?
phobos.a: Phobos orbits faster than Mars rotates (~7 h 39 min), so it rises in the west and sets in the east.

dustStorm.q: Can dust storms cover the entire planet Mars?
dustStorm.a: Yes: planet-encircling storms can dim sunlight for weeks, even though wind dynamic pressure remains low due to thin air.

moonTemp.q: What extreme temperatures does a lunar rover face?
moonTemp.a: With no atmosphere, the surface swings from ~390 K (+117 °C) in sunlight to ~100 K (-173 °C) during lunar night.

moonFootprints.q: Why are Apollo footprints still intact after more than 50 years?
moonFootprints.a: The Moon has no wind or rain; only gradual micrometeorite impacts erode regolith over millions of years.

moonDay.q: How long is a full solar day on the Moon?
moonDay.a: About 29.5 Earth days (~14 days of sunlight followed by ~14 days of darkness), requiring robust energy storage.

atacamaRovers.q: Why has NASA tested rover prototypes in the Atacama Desert?
atacamaRovers.a: Because of extreme hyperaridity, saline soils, high UV flux, and near-zero vegetation in sectors like Yungay.

perchlorate.q: Which chemical compound do Atacama and Mars soils share?
perchlorate.a: Both contain natural perchlorates and salts, valuable for studying regolith chemistry and extremophile limits.

quickQuiz.question: If we send a 100 kg rover to {{body}}, what changes compared to Antofagasta?
quickQuiz.optA: Its mass drops and slope stops mattering
quickQuiz.optB: Its mass stays 100 kg, while its weight in N drops
quickQuiz.tryAgain: Almost — remember the difference between mass (kg) and weight (N).
quickQuiz.explanation: On {{body}} gravity is ~{{pct}}% of Earth: mass stays {{mass}} kg, while weight drops from {{earthN}} N to {{bodyN}} N.
